xIqDG8slYHE.title: Moderation #8: Hanzalah and 'An Hour and an Hour'
xIqDG8slYHE.one_line: Hanzalah fears hypocrisy because his spiritual high fades at home; the Prophet answers that life is an hour and an hour.
xIqDG8slYHE.summary: He reads the hadith of Hanzalah from Sahih Muslim and Jami al-Tirmidhi. Abu Bakr finds Hanzalah weeping and declaring himself a hypocrite: with the Prophet, reminded of Paradise and Hellfire, it is as if they see them, but once home, wrestling with spouses, children and livelihoods, they forget much. Abu Bakr admits the same, and they go to the Prophet, who swears that if they stayed at home as they are in his gatherings, the angels would shake their hands in the streets, but rather it is an hour and an hour. He explains the word for that daily struggle: the constant friction of dealing with family, work and property. The spiritual state shapes who you are at an essential level, but life also demands getting and keeping a job, staying married, raising children and staying sane, and you must give that your full effort too. You cannot remain in a permanent spiritual high; you will lose your temper and get upset, and sometimes you step away for a moment of clarity and then return to life. Islam rejected monasticism for this reason. Some think the companions were overly pragmatic, but he argues we have simply lost our practicality. They held both: Umar wept in night prayer until it marked his face, yet lived fully engaged in the world.

outline.gist: With the Prophet they feel they see Paradise and Hell; at home, among family and property, they forget.

outline.heading: The meaning of the daily struggle with family and property

outline.heading: The angels would shake your hands, but an hour and an hour
outline.gist: If they stayed in that state they would not be human; life alternates between remembrance and worldly duty.

outline.heading: Life demands your full effort too
outline.gist: Work, marriage, children and sanity need real focus; you step away for clarity and return, which is why there is no monasticism.

outline.heading: Not too pragmatic: we have lost our practicality
outline.gist: The companions balanced deep worship, like Umar's night prayer, with full engagement in life.

outline.heading: Outro

1l0RD7Kir24.title: Moderation #9: Abdullah ibn Amr and the Rights of the Body
1l0RD7Kir24.one_line: The Prophet tells Abdullah ibn Amr to fast and break, pray and sleep: your body, eyes, wife and guests have rights over you.
1l0RD7Kir24.summary: He reads the hadith from Sahih al-Bukhari in which the Prophet asks Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As whether it is true that he fasts every day and prays all night. The Prophet tells him not to, but to fast and break his fast, pray and sleep, because his body, his eyes, his wife and his visitors all have a right over him, and that three days a month equals a lifetime of fasting since each good deed counts tenfold. Abdullah insisted he could do more, so he was allowed the fast of Dawud, every other day. In old age Abdullah wished he had taken the Prophet's concession, since he could not abandon what he had committed to. The lesson he draws is that small acts done consistently, with clarity and good intention, are better than a standard you cannot sustain for life. He adds the background: Abdullah's father had married him to a respected woman who, when asked about her husband, praised him but said he never came to her bed, because he spent his nights in prayer. Excess leaves you exhausted, absent from your spouse and less functional. Ignoring the Prophet's balance does not earn more reward; it loses both reward and functionality, so there is no reason not to follow his guidance.

28:76.ar: ۞إِنَّ قَٰرُونَ كَانَ مِن قَوۡمِ مُوسَىٰ فَبَغَىٰ عَلَيۡهِمۡۖ وَءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ مِنَ ٱلۡكُنُوزِ مَآ إِنَّ مَفَاتِحَهُۥ لَتَنُوٓأُ بِٱلۡعُصۡبَةِ أُوْلِي ٱلۡقُوَّةِ إِذۡ قَالَ لَهُۥ قَوۡمُهُۥ لَا تَفۡرَحۡۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلۡفَرِحِينَ
28:76.en: Now Korah was of Moses' folk, but he oppressed them; and We gave him so much treasure that the stores thereof would verily have been a burden for a troop of mighty men. When his own folk said unto him: Exult not; lo! Allah loveth not the exultant

28:77.ar: وَٱبۡتَغِ فِيمَآ ءَاتَىٰكَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلدَّارَ ٱلۡأٓخِرَةَۖ وَلَا تَنسَ نَصِيبَكَ مِنَ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ وَأَحۡسِن كَمَآ أَحۡسَنَ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيۡكَۖ وَلَا تَبۡغِ ٱلۡفَسَادَ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلۡمُفۡسِدِينَ
28:77.en: But seek the abode of the Hereafter in that which Allah hath given thee and neglect not thy portion of the world, and be thou kind even as Allah hath been kind to thee, and seek not corruption in the earth; lo! Allah loveth not corrupters

28:78.ar: قَالَ إِنَّمَآ أُوتِيتُهُۥ عَلَىٰ عِلۡمٍ عِندِيٓۚ أَوَلَمۡ يَعۡلَمۡ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ قَدۡ أَهۡلَكَ مِن قَبۡلِهِۦ مِنَ ٱلۡقُرُونِ مَنۡ هُوَ أَشَدُّ مِنۡهُ قُوَّةࣰ وَأَكۡثَرُ جَمۡعࣰ اۚ وَلَا يُسۡـَٔلُ عَن ذُنُوبِهِمُ ٱلۡمُجۡرِمُونَ
28:78.en: He said: I have been given it only on account of knowledge I possess. Knew he not that Allah had destroyed already of the generations before him men who were mightier than him in strength and greater in respect of following? The guilty are not questioned of their sins

28:79.ar: فَخَرَجَ عَلَىٰ قَوۡمِهِۦ فِي زِينَتِهِۦۖ قَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ يُرِيدُونَ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنۡيَا يَٰلَيۡتَ لَنَا مِثۡلَ مَآ أُوتِيَ قَٰرُونُ إِنَّهُۥ لَذُو حَظٍّ عَظِيمࣲ‏
28:79.en: Then went he forth before his people in his pomp. Those who were desirous of the life of the world said: Ah, would that we had the like of what hath been given unto Korah! Lo! he is lord of rare good fortune

28:80.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلۡعِلۡمَ وَيۡلَكُمۡ ثَوَابُ ٱللَّهِ خَيۡرࣱ لِّمَنۡ ءَامَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَٰلِحࣰ اۚ وَلَا يُلَقَّىٰهَآ إِلَّا ٱلصَّٰبِرُونَ
28:80.en: But those who had been given knowledge said: Woe unto you! The reward of Allah for him who believeth and doeth right is better, and only the steadfast will obtain it

28:81.ar: فَخَسَفۡنَا بِهِۦ وَبِدَارِهِ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ فَمَا كَانَ لَهُۥ مِن فِئَةࣲ يَنصُرُونَهُۥ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا كَانَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُنتَصِرِينَ
28:81.en: So We caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling-place. Then he had no host to help him against Allah, nor was he of those who can save themselves

28:82.ar: وَأَصۡبَحَ ٱلَّذِينَ تَمَنَّوۡاْ مَكَانَهُۥ بِٱلۡأَمۡسِ يَقُولُونَ وَيۡكَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَبۡسُطُ ٱلرِّزۡقَ لِمَن يَشَآءُ مِنۡ عِبَادِهِۦ وَيَقۡدِرُۖ لَوۡلَآ أَن مَّنَّ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيۡنَا لَخَسَفَ بِنَاۖ وَيۡكَأَنَّهُۥ لَا يُفۡلِحُ ٱلۡكَٰفِرُونَ
28:82.en: And morning found those who had coveted his place but yesterday crying: Ah, welladay! Allah enlargeth the provision for whom He will of His slaves and straiteneth it (for whom He will). If Allah had not been gracious unto us He would have caused it to swallow us (also). Ah, welladay! the disbelievers never prosper

xhtr0Uej0NE.title: Self-Value #39: Vanity ('Ujb)
xhtr0Uej0NE.one_line: Vanity is the flip side of low self-esteem; the cure is to stop claiming credit, give the spotlight to Allah and live in gratitude.
xhtr0Uej0NE.summary: He opens the four main diseases of the heart, all tied to self-value, starting with vanity. The nafs naturally swings toward superiority or inferiority; the disease begins when the heart learns to enjoy one swing. A healthy heart treats both swings as wrong and pulls back to the centre, because human worth is fixed by creation and nothing adds to or subtracts from it. Vanity is not the opposite of low self-esteem but its other face, an insecurity that must keep inflating itself. True confidence rests on the potential Allah gives every human at birth, paired with humility, and even good deeds should not raise one's sense of worth. Using the story of Qarun, who credited his wealth to his own knowledge and ended in ruin, he argues that claiming deserved credit for outcomes puts you in God's place, since you cannot know how much of any result your effort produced. He applies this to himself: his father's sacrifice, his gift for memorizing, and countless unseen circumstances. Others may credit you; you credit Allah and ask Him to credit you more. The remedy is gratitude, starting with the basics of life, treating praise and criticism as mere feedback, and dropping the vain claim that your story is special or that you would never do what others did.

outline.heading: Vanity and low self-esteem: one coin
outline.gist: The vain person is insecure; when the means of vanity disappear, it swings back to low self-esteem.

outline.heading: Red flag: drawing self-value from good deeds
outline.gist: Worship should deepen humility, not inflate worth.

outline.heading: Confidence in potential and humility should not change
outline.gist: Right worship reinforces these values; vanity is a sign of insecurity.

outline.heading: Why 'vanity' is a good translation
outline.gist: The English word keeps its religious sense from Christian tradition.

outline.heading: Vanity as insecurity about Allah-given potential
outline.gist: Every human is born with the potential for greatness and need prove nothing.

outline.heading: The spotlight on me versus true confidence
outline.gist: Vanity says I am amazing; confidence knows the potential is there even when struggling.

outline.heading: Iblis began with vanity
outline.gist: The Quran shows his arrogance, but it started with vanity.

outline.heading: Qarun: the wealthy man of Musa's people
outline.gist: He transgressed against his own people by taking more than his due.

outline.heading: 'Do not exult': joy or vanity
outline.gist: The same word means joy and vanity; the question is whether the emotion is genuine.

outline.heading: The advice of his people's scholars
outline.gist: Seek the Hereafter with what you have and be excellent to others as Allah was to you.

outline.heading: 'I was given it because of my knowledge'
outline.gist: Qarun credited his wealth entirely to his own expertise and work.

outline.heading: His end and the onlookers' regret
outline.gist: Those who envied him praised Allah when they saw his ruin.

outline.heading: The devil comes at the summit
outline.gist: Moments of glory are when the nafs swings furthest; he will not judge others' work.

outline.heading: His own example: outcomes could have differed
outline.gist: He worked, but cannot claim he deserves his outcomes; countless circumstances shaped them.

outline.heading: What Allah gave him that he did not earn
outline.gist: A father who dedicated his life to his learning, a gift for memorizing, and an effort that Allah let succeed.

outline.heading: Claiming credit is taking God's position
outline.gist: No one enters Paradise by deeds alone; deciding your own worth is judging for yourself.

outline.heading: Not about earning your wage
outline.gist: Employees count hours; this is about self-worth, not pay.

outline.heading: The correction: send the spotlight upward
outline.gist: See every good as a blessing; if you put a number on your share, you are vain.

outline.heading: Acceptance is Allah crediting you
outline.gist: Declaring your deeds accepted speaks on Allah's behalf.

outline.heading: The solution is gratitude
outline.gist: The first word of salah is alhamdulillah, and a whole posture is devoted to praise.

outline.heading: You credit me; I credit Allah
outline.gist: Others should thank and credit, while the person credits Allah: each side's duty.

outline.heading: The world does the opposite
outline.gist: People discredit others and claim credit for themselves.

outline.heading: Praise and criticism as feedback
outline.gist: Neither changes his worth; he takes both to improve, and is amused by the predictable critic.

outline.heading: Confidence solidifies when achievement is detached
outline.gist: Potential stays; the nafs uses accomplishments to feel full.

outline.heading: 'How dare he say it's all me'
outline.gist: There is a part that is yours, but you do not know how much.

outline.heading: How do I thank You when thanking is a blessing?
outline.gist: Recognizing that even gratitude is a gift is true gratitude.

outline.heading: Gratitude for the basics
outline.gist: The Quran points to life, Islam, consciousness, sun, moon and mountains rather than details.

outline.heading: Entitlement: is your story special?
outline.gist: Most people feel they deserve to be spared the trials others face.

outline.heading: Trading Places
outline.gist: The film shows how much of who we are is circumstance.

outline.heading: 'I would never do that' is vanity
outline.gist: Say instead alhamdulillah that Allah showed you it was wrong.

outline.heading: Ask Allah to credit you with more
outline.gist: Thank Allah for being freed from racism or hatred; ask for credit and mercy, not claim it.

12:13.ar: قَالَ إِنِّي لَيَحۡزُنُنِيٓ أَن تَذۡهَبُواْ بِهِۦ وَأَخَافُ أَن يَأۡكُلَهُ ٱلذِّئۡبُ وَأَنتُمۡ عَنۡهُ غَٰفِلُونَ
12:13.en: He said: Lo! in truth it saddens me that ye should take him with you, and I fear less the wolf devour him while ye are heedless of him

12:14.ar: قَالُواْ لَئِنۡ أَكَلَهُ ٱلذِّئۡبُ وَنَحۡنُ عُصۡبَةٌ إِنَّآ إِذࣰ ا لَّخَٰسِرُونَ
12:14.en: They said: If the wolf should devour him when we are (so strong) a band, then surely we should have already perished

12:15.ar: فَلَمَّا ذَهَبُواْ بِهِۦ وَأَجۡمَعُوٓاْ أَن يَجۡعَلُوهُ فِي غَيَٰبَتِ ٱلۡجُبِّۚ وَأَوۡحَيۡنَآ إِلَيۡهِ لَتُنَبِّئَنَّهُم بِأَمۡرِهِمۡ هَٰذَا وَهُمۡ لَا يَشۡعُرُونَ
12:15.en: Then, when they led him off, and were of one mind that they should place him in the depth of the pit, We inspired in him: Thou wilt tell them of this deed of theirs when they know (thee) not

12:16.en: And they came weeping to their father in the evening

12:17.ar: قَالُواْ يَٰٓأَبَانَآ إِنَّا ذَهَبۡنَا نَسۡتَبِقُ وَتَرَكۡنَا يُوسُفَ عِندَ مَتَٰعِنَا فَأَكَلَهُ ٱلذِّئۡبُۖ وَمَآ أَنتَ بِمُؤۡمِنࣲ لَّنَا وَلَوۡ كُنَّا صَٰدِقِينَ
12:17.en: Saying: O our father! We went racing one with another, and left Joseph by our things, and the wolf devoured him, and thou believest not our saying even when we speak the truth

12:23.ar: وَرَٰوَدَتۡهُ ٱلَّتِي هُوَ فِي بَيۡتِهَا عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦ وَغَلَّقَتِ ٱلۡأَبۡوَٰبَ وَقَالَتۡ هَيۡتَ لَكَۚ قَالَ مَعَاذَ ٱللَّهِۖ إِنَّهُۥ رَبِّيٓ أَحۡسَنَ مَثۡوَايَۖ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُفۡلِحُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ
12:23.en: And she, in whose house he was, asked of him an evil act. She bolted the doors and said: Come! He said: I seek refuge in Allah! Lo! he is my lord, who hath treated me honourably. Lo! wrong-doers never prosper

12:24.ar: وَلَقَدۡ هَمَّتۡ بِهِۦۖ وَهَمَّ بِهَا لَوۡلَآ أَن رَّءَا بُرۡهَٰنَ رَبِّهِۦۚ كَذَٰلِكَ لِنَصۡرِفَ عَنۡهُ ٱلسُّوٓءَ وَٱلۡفَحۡشَآءَۚ إِنَّهُۥ مِنۡ عِبَادِنَا ٱلۡمُخۡلَصِينَ
12:24.en: She verily desired him, and he would have desired her if it had not been that he saw the argument of his Lord. Thus it was, that We might ward off from him evil and lewdness. Lo! he was of Our chosen slaves

12:25.ar: وَٱسۡتَبَقَا ٱلۡبَابَ وَقَدَّتۡ قَمِيصَهُۥ مِن دُبُرࣲ وَأَلۡفَيَا سَيِّدَهَا لَدَا ٱلۡبَابِۚ قَالَتۡ مَا جَزَآءُ مَنۡ أَرَادَ بِأَهۡلِكَ سُوٓءًا إِلَّآ أَن يُسۡجَنَ أَوۡ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمࣱ‏
12:25.en: And they raced with one another to the door, and she tore his shirt from behind, and they met her lord and master at the door. She said: What shall be his reward, who wisheth evil to thy folk, save prison or a painful doom

12:26.ar: قَالَ هِيَ رَٰوَدَتۡنِي عَن نَّفۡسِيۚ وَشَهِدَ شَاهِدࣱ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِهَآ إِن كَانَ قَمِيصُهُۥ قُدَّ مِن قُبُلࣲ فَصَدَقَتۡ وَهُوَ مِنَ ٱلۡكَٰذِبِينَ
12:26.en: (Joseph) said: She it was who asked of me an evil act. And a witness of her own folk testified: If his shirt is torn from before, then she speaketh truth and he is of the liars

12:27.ar: وَإِن كَانَ قَمِيصُهُۥ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرࣲ فَكَذَبَتۡ وَهُوَ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ
12:27.en: And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she hath lied and he is of the truthful

12:28.ar: فَلَمَّا رَءَا قَمِيصَهُۥ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرࣲ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ مِن كَيۡدِكُنَّۖ إِنَّ كَيۡدَكُنَّ عَظِيمࣱ‏
12:28.en: So when he saw his shirt torn from behind, he said: Lo! this is of the guile of you women. Lo! the guile of you is very great

12:29.ar: يُوسُفُ أَعۡرِضۡ عَنۡ هَٰذَاۚ وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرِي لِذَنۢبِكِۖ إِنَّكِ كُنتِ مِنَ ٱلۡخَاطِـِٔينَ
12:29.en: O Joseph! Turn away from this, and thou, (O woman), ask forgiveness for thy sin. Lo! thou art of the faulty

12:30.ar: ۞وَقَالَ نِسۡوَةࣱ فِي ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ ٱمۡرَأَتُ ٱلۡعَزِيزِ تُرَٰوِدُ فَتَىٰهَا عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦۖ قَدۡ شَغَفَهَا حُبًّاۖ إِنَّا لَنَرَىٰهَا فِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
12:30.en: And women in the city said: The ruler's wife is asking of her slave-boy an ill-deed. Indeed he has smitten her to the heart with love. We behold her in plain aberration

12:31.ar: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتۡ بِمَكۡرِهِنَّ أَرۡسَلَتۡ إِلَيۡهِنَّ وَأَعۡتَدَتۡ لَهُنَّ مُتَّكَـࣰٔ ا وَءَاتَتۡ كُلَّ وَٰحِدَةࣲ مِّنۡهُنَّ سِكِّينࣰ ا وَقَالَتِ ٱخۡرُجۡ عَلَيۡهِنَّۖ فَلَمَّا رَأَيۡنَهُۥٓ أَكۡبَرۡنَهُۥ وَقَطَّعۡنَ أَيۡدِيَهُنَّ وَقُلۡنَ حَٰشَ لِلَّهِ مَا هَٰذَا بَشَرًا إِنۡ هَٰذَآ إِلَّا مَلَكࣱ كَرِيمࣱ‏
12:31.en: And when she heard of their sly talk, she sent to them and prepared for them a cushioned couch (to lie on at the feast) and gave to every one of them a knife and said (to Joseph): Come out unto them! And when they saw him they exalted him and cut their hands, exclaiming: Allah Blameless! This is no a human being. This is not other than some gracious angel

12:32.ar: قَالَتۡ فَذَٰلِكُنَّ ٱلَّذِي لُمۡتُنَّنِي فِيهِۖ وَلَقَدۡ رَٰوَدتُّهُۥ عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦ فَٱسۡتَعۡصَمَۖ وَلَئِن لَّمۡ يَفۡعَلۡ مَآ ءَامُرُهُۥ لَيُسۡجَنَنَّ وَلَيَكُونࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلصَّٰغِرِينَ
12:32.en: She said: This is he on whose account ye blamed me. I asked of him an evil act, but he proved continent, but if he do not my behest he verily shall be imprisoned, and verily shall be of those brought low

12:33.ar: قَالَ رَبِّ ٱلسِّجۡنُ أَحَبُّ إِلَيَّ مِمَّا يَدۡعُونَنِيٓ إِلَيۡهِۖ وَإِلَّا تَصۡرِفۡ عَنِّي كَيۡدَهُنَّ أَصۡبُ إِلَيۡهِنَّ وَأَكُن مِّنَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِينَ
12:33.en: He said: O my Lord! Prison is more dear than that unto which they urge me, and if Thou fend not off their wiles from me I shall incline unto them and become of the foolish

12:34.ar: فَٱسۡتَجَابَ لَهُۥ رَبُّهُۥ فَصَرَفَ عَنۡهُ كَيۡدَهُنَّۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
12:34.en: So his Lord heard his prayer and fended off their wiles from him. Lo! He is Hearer, Knower

12:35.ar: ثُمَّ بَدَا لَهُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ مَا رَأَوُاْ ٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ لَيَسۡجُنُنَّهُۥ حَتَّىٰ حِينࣲ‏
12:35.en: And it seemed good to them (the men-folk) after they had seen the signs (of his innocence) to imprison him for a time

13:38.ar: وَلَقَدۡ أَرۡسَلۡنَا رُسُلࣰ ا مِّن قَبۡلِكَ وَجَعَلۡنَا لَهُمۡ أَزۡوَٰجࣰ ا وَذُرِّيَّةࣰۚ وَمَا كَانَ لِرَسُولٍ أَن يَأۡتِيَ بِـَٔايَةٍ إِلَّا بِإِذۡنِ ٱللَّهِۗ لِكُلِّ أَجَلࣲ كِتَابࣱ‏
13:38.en: And verily We sent messengers (to mankind) before thee, and We appointed for them wives and offspring, and it was not (given) to any messenger that he should bring a portent save by Allah's leave. For everything there is a time prescribed

6:67.en: For every announcement there is a term, and ye will come to know

4:76.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِۖ وَٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱلطَّٰغُوتِ فَقَٰتِلُوٓاْ أَوۡلِيَآءَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِۖ إِنَّ كَيۡدَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِ كَانَ ضَعِيفًا
4:76.en: Those who believe do battle for the cause of Allah; and those who disbelieve do battle for the cause of idols. So fight the minions of the devil. Lo! the devil's strategy is ever weak

3:103.ar: وَٱعۡتَصِمُواْ بِحَبۡلِ ٱللَّهِ جَمِيعࣰ ا وَلَا تَفَرَّقُواْۚ وَٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡ إِذۡ كُنتُمۡ أَعۡدَآءࣰ فَأَلَّفَ بَيۡنَ قُلُوبِكُمۡ فَأَصۡبَحۡتُم بِنِعۡمَتِهِۦٓ إِخۡوَٰنࣰ ا وَكُنتُمۡ عَلَىٰ شَفَا حُفۡرَةࣲ مِّنَ ٱلنَّارِ فَأَنقَذَكُم مِّنۡهَاۗ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَهۡتَدُونَ
3:103.en: And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate. And remember Allah's favour unto you: How ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts so that ye became as brothers by His grace; and (how) ye were upon the brink of an abyss of fire, and He did save you from it. Thus Allah maketh clear His revelations unto you, that haply ye may be guided

69:45.en: We assuredly had taken him by the right hand

fTfMQhBPWR0.title: Arabic Tafsir: Surat Yusuf, Verses 23-35
fTfMQhBPWR0.one_line: Yusuf's unchanging character under three injustices, the self's hidden scheming, the women of the city, and choosing prison over sin.
fTfMQhBPWR0.summary: Completing verses 23 to 29 before moving on, the sheikh argues that morals are only real when they hold regardless of circumstances. Yusuf was wronged by his brothers, the caravan and the minister's wife before he was twenty, yet he never became a wolf; the wolf appears in the Quran only in this story, a rebuke to the idea that you must devour or be devoured. His refusal rested on certainty after seeing his Lord's proof, and on patience with a painful decree that later saved the whole region from famine. On the torn shirt he notes an early instance of evidence-based investigation, and insists the verse about great scheming concerns the human self, not women: kayd is doing one thing to achieve a hidden aim, and the nafs always slips a share for itself into every deed, so true sincerity means doing deeds in which the self has no share. In verses 30 to 35 he explains how secrets spread, the Arabic ranks of love from shaghaf to 'ubudiyyah, the banquet and the cut hands, Zulaykha's unwilling confession, and Yusuf's plea that prison is dearer to him. He calls this a stance no storyteller could invent, and stresses that Allah counted his unjust imprisonment as the answer to his prayer.

outline.heading: Morals are morals only when they hold in every condition
outline.gist: Yusuf stayed the same from childhood to maturity whatever happened to him.

outline.heading: The wolf that never appears elsewhere in the Quran
outline.gist: The wolf is mentioned only in Yusuf's story, a rebuke to the saying that you must be a wolf or be eaten; being harmed never justifies harming others.

outline.heading: Three injustices, yet 'I seek refuge in Allah'
outline.gist: Abandoned by his brothers, sold by the caravan and wronged by the minister's wife, he still refused to disobey Allah.

outline.heading: A painful decree that saved a whole region
outline.gist: Had he not been thrown in the well, no one would have interpreted the king's dream and the region would have perished in the famine; be patient with decree.

outline.heading: The proof of his Lord
outline.gist: His restraint came from clear certainty, not lack of opportunity, so Allah turned evil away from His sincere servant.

outline.heading: The torn shirt and the witness
outline.gist: Two conflicting accounts require evidence; the shirt torn from behind proves who was lying, an early model of investigation.

outline.heading: 'Your scheming is great' is about the self, not women
outline.gist: Men misuse the verse to excuse themselves; the scheming comes from the self that commands evil, which every person has.

outline.heading: What kayd means
outline.gist: Kayd is doing something outwardly aimed at one goal to secretly reach another; the wise catch their own self's scheming before it is too late.

outline.heading: The self always takes a share
outline.gist: The nafs cannot understand doing anything purely for Allah and inserts reputation, status or loyalty into every deed.

outline.heading: Learning to do deeds with no share for the self
outline.gist: Test yourself with worship no one will ever know about; the self resists it and wants to be seen.

outline.heading: The story is about human nature, and almost everyone reforms
outline.gist: Zulaykha and the brothers will reform later; only the caravan who sold a child remain wholly base.

outline.heading: 'Turn away from this' and 'seek forgiveness'
outline.gist: The minister chose to cover the matter and told his wife to seek forgiveness.

outline.heading: The Hyksos and remnants of monotheism
outline.gist: Egypt's rulers then were Canaanite Hyksos with some knowledge of God, which is why there is no Pharaoh in this surah.

outline.heading: Mukhti' versus khati'
outline.gist: One who errs while seeking the right differs from one who knowingly chooses wrong; she was called the latter.

outline.heading: The women of the city
outline.gist: Recitation of verse 30.

outline.heading: Murawadah: bargaining someone out of what they value
outline.gist: It means pressuring a person through shame or soft persuasion into giving what they do not want to give.

outline.heading: How a secret spreads
outline.gist: Only four knew, and the witness likely talked; once a secret leaves your chest it reaches the horizons, except in professions bound to confidentiality.

outline.heading: Keep secrets and cover others' faults
outline.gist: Few can keep a secret; whoever exposes his brother's faults, Allah will expose his.

outline.heading: The Arabic ranks of love
outline.gist: Shaghaf is one of many ranks of love the Arabs distinguished, as listed by al-Tha'alibi.

outline.heading: The Arabs as lovers: the poets and Ibn Abbas
outline.gist: Ibn Abbas memorized a whole poem of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah on one hearing and defended it as language and literature.

outline.heading: 'Ubudiyyah as a rank of love
outline.gist: Servitude to Allah is the rank of love in which the lover's will becomes the beloved's will.

outline.heading: Shaghaf and plain misguidance
outline.gist: His love filled the lining around her heart; her misguidance was of judgment, not religion.

outline.heading: The banquet
outline.gist: Recitation of verse 31.

outline.heading: Why their talk is called makr
outline.gist: The women gossiped on purpose so she would summon them and they could see Yusuf.

outline.heading: The reclining feast and the Prophet's manners
outline.gist: Reclining while eating was a sign of luxury; the Prophet refused to eat reclining out of humility and respect for blessings.

outline.heading: They were awed and cut their hands
outline.gist: His prophetic dignity and beauty, half of all beauty, overwhelmed them.

outline.heading: 'Hasha lillah': this is no human
outline.gist: Their words show they knew of Allah; they said he must be a noble angel.

outline.heading: Why she gathered them: no one can bear losing their circle
outline.gist: People can endure the world's criticism but not their friends' gossip, so she had to restore her standing.

outline.heading: Reciting wa-layakunan
outline.gist: The light emphatic nun is written as alif; stopping on it is permissible but weak.

outline.heading: Fa' al-fasihah: 'that is the one you blamed me for'
outline.gist: The particle compresses an implied sentence: if this is the angel you saw, he is the one you blamed me over.

outline.heading: She could not lie about him
outline.gist: Though people prefer to be the pursued, his innocence was so clear that she confessed she pursued him; some good remained in her.

outline.heading: Fasta'sam: he sealed himself off
outline.gist: He held fast to Allah's protection and left her no opening at all.

outline.heading: The threat of prison and humiliation
outline.gist: She swore that if he refused he would be jailed and brought low.

outline.heading: 'Prison is dearer to me': a line no storyteller could invent
outline.gist: Now all the women sought him, and he still preferred prison.

outline.heading: A young slave pursued by many
outline.gist: He had no wealth or status to lose, yet he refused everything offered.

outline.heading: Sababah and jahl
outline.gist: Sababah is the first stirring of desire; jahl here means base, unmanly conduct, as in Amr ibn Kulthum's verse.

outline.heading: Even the sincere feel weakness
outline.gist: Despite his resolve he admitted he felt the start of weakness and asked Allah to protect him.

outline.heading: Each person chooses his stance
outline.gist: Some young men would trade years in prison for one night; Yusuf chose prison over sin, and each of us chooses our values.

outline.heading: The Casanova model versus the prophets
outline.gist: He could have lived like a womanizer of Western legend, yet chose prison, the worst of worldly hardships, unjustly.

outline.heading: His Lord answered him
outline.gist: You do not dictate when Allah answers; everyone has moments when Allah rescued them, then they forget.

outline.heading: Layasjununnahu: the grammar
outline.gist: A common recitation error, and how the emphatic nun produced the doubled nun.

outline.heading: 'After they had seen the signs'
outline.gist: Ayat in the Quran usually means evidences; seeing no way out, the household decided to jail him.

outline.heading: Scapegoated and paraded
outline.gist: They cast him as the attacker so the women would appear chaste; some reports say he was paraded through the streets.

outline.heading: Unjust prison as Allah's answer
outline.gist: Jailed for years for refusing sin, he could have despaired, yet Allah called his imprisonment the answer to his prayer.

outline.heading: Outro

4:49.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ إِلَى ٱلَّذِينَ يُزَكُّونَ أَنفُسَهُمۚ بَلِ ٱللَّهُ يُزَكِّي مَن يَشَآءُ وَلَا يُظۡلَمُونَ فَتِيلًا
4:49.en: Hast thou not seen those who praise themselves for purity? Nay, Allah purifieth whom He will, and they will not be wronged even the hair upon a date-stone

29:2.ar: أَحَسِبَ ٱلنَّاسُ أَن يُتۡرَكُوٓاْ أَن يَقُولُوٓاْ ءَامَنَّا وَهُمۡ لَا يُفۡتَنُونَ
29:2.en: Do men imagine that they will be left (at ease) because they say, We believe, and will not be tested with affliction

PXe6dM3_bq4.title: Self-Value #40: Vanity, Entitlement, Expectations and Mediocrity
PXe6dM3_bq4.one_line: Vanity as claiming credit for good outcomes, and how it feeds entitlement before Allah, inflated expectations, and fear of real effort.
PXe6dM3_bq4.summary: Continuing on vanity, which the Prophet named among three destructive things, the sheikh defines it as claiming credit for your share in good outcomes. Since each of us is a recipe of upbringing, gifts, teachers and Allah's facilitation, no one knows his own share, so praise goes to Allah, while others are credited with good assumption; tazkiyah is applied to yourself, never to others. He then draws out two roots. Entitlement: before Allah we deserve nothing, since life itself is an unpayable debt; the only worldly promises are trials and, for those who live rightly, serenity. He compares the entitled believer to a spoiled child or a debtor demanding a further loan, and prescribes gratitude. Expectations: keep them modest with people, high for yourself, and have none of Allah, only hope and dua. Finally, vanity breeds mediocrity: unwilling to be seen giving our best and falling short, we hold back, joke around, or ignore criticism. He urges investing the heart rather than the ego in work, seeking honest feedback, pursuing truth over validation, and replacing the need for vanity with confidence in one's Allah-given potential and gratitude.

outline.gist: Allah usually leaves His gifts with us hoping we notice; anything extra is a bonus, and gratitude brings more.

outline.heading: Holding back as a defence; growth through critique

outline.heading: Give honest feedback, kindly

outline.heading: A Muslim pursues truth, not validation
outline.gist: We change our theory of existence to Islam's, not search Islam for support of our theory.

outline.heading: Replacing the need for vanity: confidence and gratitude

BnmSmVFqPqk.title: Moderation #12: Ruined Are the Extremists
BnmSmVFqPqk.one_line: The hadith 'ruined are the mutanatti'un': those who complicate an easy deen, and the opposite camp that empties it.
BnmSmVFqPqk.summary: Continuing his series on moderation, the sheikh explains the hadith in Sahih Muslim in which the Prophet said three times that the mutanatti'un are ruined. He first explains the idiom as a phrase of censure, almost a wish that such a group would cease to exist, and admits the narration has little surrounding context. He then unpacks the word: it comes from the upper palate, the source of certain emphatic letters, and describes someone who speaks from the top of the mouth to sound clever, complicating what is simple. Religiously, these are people who look for difficulty inside what was designed for ease and exaggerate every practice, ruining the beauty of the deen. He notes this appeared decades after the Prophet, with the Khawarij, causing fitnah and division that persists. What he finds striking is that the loudest critics of extremism are often those who have hollowed Islam out and cherry-pick it, and each camp justifies itself by pointing at the other. The prophetic way lies between them, and he asks everyone to watch that they fall into neither.

outline.gist: Said three times; an Arab expression wishing a blameworthy group would perish.

outline.gist: No parallel narrations explain the occasion, but the wording itself teaches.

outline.gist: One who complicates simple things to sound clever.

m26IK5Bcx_s.title: Moderation #10: Zaynab's Rope and the Reversed Dynamic
m26IK5Bcx_s.one_line: The Prophet removes a rope used to prolong night prayer: worship that breaks your functioning earns less, and today the dynamic runs backwards.
m26IK5Bcx_s.summary: He takes the hadith in which the Prophet entered the masjid, found a rope tied between two pillars and learned that Zaynab used it to hold herself up when she tired in prayer. Before the ruling he draws two observations: women of the Prophet's household were present in the masjid often enough to set something up there without fear of reproach, and the companions' instinct was always how to do more, even inventing a tool to pray beyond their physical limit. The Prophet ordered it taken down: pray while you have energy and sit when you tire. Worship pushed to the point that it destroys your sleep and your ability to be a good spouse, parent, worker and friend actually yields less reward over time. He links this to a pattern he has watched for two decades: people returning to Allah after a long absence take on far too much, burn out within months and fall back. Habits and longevity are built through balance. Finally he notes how the dynamic has flipped. The Prophet had to tell his companions to slow down, eat, sleep and rest, while imams today must plead with people to attend anything. Then people chose the safer opinion and the Prophet offered ease; now people ask the imam for the easy answer. He asks his listeners to want the safer option for themselves, and to pick up their effort a little.

outline.gist: The Prophet enters the masjid and finds a rope he had not seen before.

outline.heading: Zaynab's rope for long prayer
outline.gist: It belonged to Zaynab, most likely his daughter, who held it when she tired standing in prayer.

outline.heading: Women's presence in the masjid and the companions' drive to do more
outline.gist: Women came often enough to set this up safely, and their instinct was always how to worship more than the body allows.

outline.heading: Take it down: pray with your energy, sit when tired
outline.gist: Worship that ruins sleep and daily duties brings less reward in the long run.

outline.heading: Returners who come in hot and burn out
outline.gist: From long observation, those who repent take on too much, burn out and relapse; habits need balance to last.

outline.heading: The dynamic has reversed
outline.gist: The Prophet had to slow people down, while today the imam begs people to show up at all.

outline.heading: Seek the safer opinion; the scholar offers the easier one
outline.gist: The questioner should want caution for himself while the scholar gives the easiest well-evidenced answer; we may need to balance by doing more.

outline.heading: Outro

TX9Ffu08NXk.title: Moderation #4: Saddidu wa Qaribu
TX9Ffu08NXk.one_line: Unpacking the two-word prophetic command saddidu wa qaribu: approach with balance and hit the objective.
TX9Ffu08NXk.summary: The sheikh calls this the most powerful hadith on moderation: the Prophet's two-word instruction, saddidu wa qaribu. He breaks down each word from its root. Qaribu, linked to the word for a small boat that must be kept balanced or it flips, means approach with balance. Saddidu, a word he knew from childhood football cartoons, means to strike so the ball goes into the goal: kicking too hard overshoots and too softly falls short, so the point is hitting the objective, not maximum force. A person who is sadid is functional and actually achieves things, unlike someone who exhausts himself with nothing to show. The companions heard these two words and understood at once that the religion is not about extravagance, exaggeration or being the loudest. He applies it to giving advice: before correcting a brother, think about how he will react, whether you are the right person to say it, and how to say it so that he actually changes. Anyone can say what they want; sincerity is approaching with balance so the objective is reached. This, he says, was the method of the Prophet and must become ours.

outline.gist: Introduces the hadith saddidu wa qaribu as the most powerful on moderation and a sign of the Prophet's concise eloquence.

EHuZ8cK6340.title: Moderation #13: Entrusting to Allah When Someone Travels
EHuZ8cK6340.one_line: Closing the Moderation series with two prophetic farewell formulas that entrust a traveller's faith and family to Allah.
EHuZ8cK6340.summary: Having finished what he wanted to say on balance and moderation, the sheikh closes the series with two short narrations for moments of parting. In the first, from Ibn Umar in al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet would bid a departing man farewell by entrusting to Allah his religion, his trusts and the final outcome of his deeds. In the second, from Abu Hurayrah in Ibn al-Sunni's work on daily supplications, the traveller says to his family: I entrust you to Allah, whose trusts are never lost. He explains that whatever Allah guards is never lost and never disappoints those He protects, and that the formula is a way of remembering that we move through the world under His care. He reflects that a single moment means different things to different people: some are living their happiest moment and others their worst. He asks the audience to use both formulas whenever someone leaves or when they themselves leave, as a reminder that Allah is the protector and provider.

eMvmruJrvFg.title: Moderation #7: The Religion Is Ease
eMvmruJrvFg.one_line: The hadith that the deen is ease: Islam is not built on difficulty, and the right thing is not always the hardest thing.
eMvmruJrvFg.summary: He continues the series on balance by restating its core rule: everything in Islam is meant to reach its objective through balance, and the moment anything is exaggerated it stops working and extremism takes its place, whether through doing too much or too little. He then takes the hadith that the religion is ease and that no one makes it hard without being overcome by it. Islam is not philosophically rooted in difficulty: its goal is ease and its preferred method is the easiest path, provided no ethic, principle or prohibition is compromised. Holding to principle will often make the road harder than the haram alternative, but hardship is a by-product, not the aim. He applies this to how we teach children: tell them they do something because it is right, not because it is hard, and within the right options choose the easiest. Anyone who plays tug-of-war with the deen to make it harder than it is will lose. His central correction is that the difficult thing and the right thing are often the same but not synonymous. The question in each moment is what is most correct, and if there is an easier way to do it, take it, never choosing difficulty for its own sake.

outline.heading: Balance keeps everything functional; extremism runs both ways
outline.gist: Exaggerating anything breaks its function, and extremism can mean too much or too little.

outline.heading: The deen is rooted in ease, not difficulty
outline.gist: Islam's goal and its method are ease; difficulties come, but they are not the philosophy.

outline.heading: The easiest path within principle, and teaching children
outline.gist: Choose the easiest option that keeps ethics and halal intact; tell children they act because it is right, not because it is hard.

outline.heading: Whoever makes the deen hard is overcome by it
outline.gist: The tug-of-war image from the hadith: the ease of Islam prevails over those who over-burden it.

outline.heading: Difficult and right are not synonymous
outline.gist: Aim for the most correct act, take ease where it exists, and never seek hardship for its own sake.

12:33.ar: قَالَ رَبِّ ٱلسِّجۡنُ أَحَبُّ إِلَيَّ مِمَّا يَدۡعُونَنِيٓ إِلَيۡهِۖ وَإِلَّا تَصۡرِفۡ عَنِّي كَيۡدَهُنَّ أَصۡبُ إِلَيۡهِنَّ وَأَكُن مِّنَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِينَ
12:33.en: He said: O my Lord! Prison is more dear than that unto which they urge me, and if Thou fend not off their wiles from me I shall incline unto them and become of the foolish

12:34.ar: فَٱسۡتَجَابَ لَهُۥ رَبُّهُۥ فَصَرَفَ عَنۡهُ كَيۡدَهُنَّۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
12:34.en: So his Lord heard his prayer and fended off their wiles from him. Lo! He is Hearer, Knower

12:35.ar: ثُمَّ بَدَا لَهُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ مَا رَأَوُاْ ٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ لَيَسۡجُنُنَّهُۥ حَتَّىٰ حِينࣲ‏
12:35.en: And it seemed good to them (the men-folk) after they had seen the signs (of his innocence) to imprison him for a time

12:36.ar: وَدَخَلَ مَعَهُ ٱلسِّجۡنَ فَتَيَانِۖ قَالَ أَحَدُهُمَآ إِنِّيٓ أَرَىٰنِيٓ أَعۡصِرُ خَمۡرࣰ اۖ وَقَالَ ٱلۡأٓخَرُ إِنِّيٓ أَرَىٰنِيٓ أَحۡمِلُ فَوۡقَ رَأۡسِي خُبۡزࣰ ا تَأۡكُلُ ٱلطَّيۡرُ مِنۡهُۖ نَبِّئۡنَا بِتَأۡوِيلِهِۦٓۖ إِنَّا نَرَىٰكَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
12:36.en: And two young men went to prison with him. One of them said: I dreamed that I was pressing wine. The other said: I dreamed that I was carrying upon my head bread whereof the birds were eating. Announce unto us the interpretation, for we see thee of those good (at interpretation)

12:37.ar: قَالَ لَا يَأۡتِيكُمَا طَعَامࣱ تُرۡزَقَانِهِۦٓ إِلَّا نَبَّأۡتُكُمَا بِتَأۡوِيلِهِۦ قَبۡلَ أَن يَأۡتِيَكُمَاۚ ذَٰلِكُمَا مِمَّا عَلَّمَنِي رَبِّيٓۚ إِنِّي تَرَكۡتُ مِلَّةَ قَوۡمࣲ لَّا يُؤۡمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَهُم بِٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ هُمۡ كَٰفِرُونَ
12:37.en: He said: The food which ye are given (daily) shall not come unto you but I shall tell you the interpretation ere it cometh unto you. This is of that which my Lord hath taught me. Lo! I have forsaken the religion of folk who believe not in Allah and are disbelievers in the Hereafter

12:38.ar: وَٱتَّبَعۡتُ مِلَّةَ ءَابَآءِيٓ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ وَإِسۡحَٰقَ وَيَعۡقُوبَۚ مَا كَانَ لَنَآ أَن نُّشۡرِكَ بِٱللَّهِ مِن شَيۡءࣲۚ ذَٰلِكَ مِن فَضۡلِ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡنَا وَعَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَٰكِنَّ أَكۡثَرَ ٱلنَّاسِ لَا يَشۡكُرُونَ
12:38.en: And I have followed the religion of my fathers, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob. It never was for us to attribute aught as partner to Allah. This is of the bounty of Allah unto us (the seed of Abraham) and unto mankind; but most men give not thanks

12:23.ar: وَرَٰوَدَتۡهُ ٱلَّتِي هُوَ فِي بَيۡتِهَا عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦ وَغَلَّقَتِ ٱلۡأَبۡوَٰبَ وَقَالَتۡ هَيۡتَ لَكَۚ قَالَ مَعَاذَ ٱللَّهِۖ إِنَّهُۥ رَبِّيٓ أَحۡسَنَ مَثۡوَايَۖ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُفۡلِحُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ
12:23.en: And she, in whose house he was, asked of him an evil act. She bolted the doors and said: Come! He said: I seek refuge in Allah! Lo! he is my lord, who hath treated me honourably. Lo! wrong-doers never prosper

12:32.ar: قَالَتۡ فَذَٰلِكُنَّ ٱلَّذِي لُمۡتُنَّنِي فِيهِۖ وَلَقَدۡ رَٰوَدتُّهُۥ عَن نَّفۡسِهِۦ فَٱسۡتَعۡصَمَۖ وَلَئِن لَّمۡ يَفۡعَلۡ مَآ ءَامُرُهُۥ لَيُسۡجَنَنَّ وَلَيَكُونࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلصَّٰغِرِينَ
12:32.en: She said: This is he on whose account ye blamed me. I asked of him an evil act, but he proved continent, but if he do not my behest he verily shall be imprisoned, and verily shall be of those brought low

14:27.ar: يُثَبِّتُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ بِٱلۡقَوۡلِ ٱلثَّابِتِ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا وَفِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِۖ وَيُضِلُّ ٱللَّهُ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَۚ وَيَفۡعَلُ ٱللَّهُ مَا يَشَآءُ
14:27.en: Allah confirmeth those who believe by a firm saying in the life of the world and in the Hereafter, and Allah sendeth wrong-doers astray. And Allah doeth what He will

12:22.ar: وَلَمَّا بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُۥٓ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ حُكۡمࣰ ا وَعِلۡمࣰ اۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نَجۡزِي ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
12:22.en: And And when he reached his prime We gave him wisdom and knowledge. Thus We reward the good

18:79.ar: أَمَّا ٱلسَّفِينَةُ فَكَانَتۡ لِمَسَٰكِينَ يَعۡمَلُونَ فِي ٱلۡبَحۡرِ فَأَرَدتُّ أَنۡ أَعِيبَهَا وَكَانَ وَرَآءَهُم مَّلِكࣱ يَأۡخُذُ كُلَّ سَفِينَةٍ غَصۡبࣰ ا
18:79.en: As for the ship, it belonged to poor people working on the river, and I wished to mar it, for there was a king behind them who is taking every ship by force

18:80.ar: وَأَمَّا ٱلۡغُلَٰمُ فَكَانَ أَبَوَاهُ مُؤۡمِنَيۡنِ فَخَشِينَآ أَن يُرۡهِقَهُمَا طُغۡيَٰنࣰ ا وَكُفۡرࣰ ا
18:80.en: And as for the lad, his parents were believers and we feared lest he should oppress them by rebellion and disbelief

18:81.ar: فَأَرَدۡنَآ أَن يُبۡدِلَهُمَا رَبُّهُمَا خَيۡرࣰ ا مِّنۡهُ زَكَوٰةࣰ وَأَقۡرَبَ رُحۡمࣰ ا
18:81.en: And we intended that their Lord should change him for them for one better in purity and nearer to mercy

12:42.ar: وَقَالَ لِلَّذِي ظَنَّ أَنَّهُۥ نَاجࣲ مِّنۡهُمَا ٱذۡكُرۡنِي عِندَ رَبِّكَ فَأَنسَىٰهُ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ ذِكۡرَ رَبِّهِۦ فَلَبِثَ فِي ٱلسِّجۡنِ بِضۡعَ سِنِينَ
12:42.en: And he said unto him of the twain who he knew would be released: Mention me in the presence of thy lord. But Satan caused him to forget to mention it to his lord, so he (Joseph) stayed in prison for some years

12:11.ar: قَالُواْ يَٰٓأَبَانَا مَا لَكَ لَا تَأۡمَ۬نَّا عَلَىٰ يُوسُفَ وَإِنَّا لَهُۥ لَنَٰصِحُونَ
12:11.en: They said: O our father! Why wilt thou not trust us with Joseph, when lo! we are good friends to him

12:12.ar: أَرۡسِلۡهُ مَعَنَا غَدࣰ ا يَرۡتَعۡ وَيَلۡعَبۡ وَإِنَّا لَهُۥ لَحَٰفِظُونَ
12:12.en: Send him with us to-morrow that he may enjoy himself and play. And lo! we shall take good care of him

12:13.ar: قَالَ إِنِّي لَيَحۡزُنُنِيٓ أَن تَذۡهَبُواْ بِهِۦ وَأَخَافُ أَن يَأۡكُلَهُ ٱلذِّئۡبُ وَأَنتُمۡ عَنۡهُ غَٰفِلُونَ
12:13.en: He said: Lo! in truth it saddens me that ye should take him with you, and I fear less the wolf devour him while ye are heedless of him

12:14.ar: قَالُواْ لَئِنۡ أَكَلَهُ ٱلذِّئۡبُ وَنَحۡنُ عُصۡبَةٌ إِنَّآ إِذࣰ ا لَّخَٰسِرُونَ
12:14.en: They said: If the wolf should devour him when we are (so strong) a band, then surely we should have already perished

93:3.en: Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee

93:4.en: And verily the latter portion will be better for thee than the former

93:5.en: And verily thy Lord will give unto thee so that thou wilt be content

12:26.ar: قَالَ هِيَ رَٰوَدَتۡنِي عَن نَّفۡسِيۚ وَشَهِدَ شَاهِدࣱ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِهَآ إِن كَانَ قَمِيصُهُۥ قُدَّ مِن قُبُلࣲ فَصَدَقَتۡ وَهُوَ مِنَ ٱلۡكَٰذِبِينَ
12:26.en: (Joseph) said: She it was who asked of me an evil act. And a witness of her own folk testified: If his shirt is torn from before, then she speaketh truth and he is of the liars

12:27.ar: وَإِن كَانَ قَمِيصُهُۥ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرࣲ فَكَذَبَتۡ وَهُوَ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ
12:27.en: And if his shirt is torn from behind, then she hath lied and he is of the truthful

fYbUqC0Lqig.title: Arabic Tafseer: Surah Yusuf 12:33-38
fYbUqC0Lqig.one_line: Yusuf chooses prison over sin, Allah answers his prayer through prison, and in prison his first act is calling two young men to Allah.
fYbUqC0Lqig.summary: The sheikh resumes Surah Yusuf at Yusuf's prayer that prison is dearer to him than what the women call him to. Even a purified soul stays human and weak, as the story of Abdullah ibn Hudhafah shows, and sin arrives by small steps, so Yusuf feared even inclining toward them. Allah answered him, yet the answer was years of unjust imprisonment, which leads to his central point: we often cannot tell mercy from punishment, as with Khidr's ship and the boy. The surah's aim is moral steadfastness: ethics admit no 'considerations' the way fiqh does, so a sinner should repent plainly instead of justifying himself, and Muslims should stop fighting over fiqh while neglecting agreed morals. Reading 12:36-38, he discusses prison in Islamic law and today's failing prisons, the conditions for a true dream, ihsan as visible competence, and ta'wil as interpretation. Yusuf asks the two young men for a moment before answering, attributes his knowledge to Allah, and calls them to Allah rather than complaining. He closes on 12:38: morality cannot survive without a creedal foundation, and societies that keep the ethics while dropping the belief eventually lose both.

outline.heading: Recap: refusing many women, Yusuf turns to his Lord
outline.gist: He refused not only the minister's wife but other women who pursued him.

outline.heading: Prison is dearer to me: the proof he had internalized
outline.gist: The proof of his Lord was a settled understanding that bred fear of Allah and sincerity.

outline.heading: Even the purified remain human and weak
outline.gist: Tazkiyah frees one from being ruled by instinct but does not erase human needs and weakness.

outline.heading: Abdullah ibn Hudhafah before the Byzantine king
outline.gist: He refused pork and wine as a leader, ignored the woman sent to him, and wept only for deeds he had missed.

outline.heading: Yusuf senses his own weakness
outline.gist: Young and wronged, he asks Allah to turn their plot away lest he incline.

outline.heading: 'Lest I incline': sin comes by steps
outline.gist: No one falls at once; soft speech, flirting, online chats, photos and outings come first.

outline.heading: Judgment and knowledge; ignorance of action
outline.gist: Yusuf's self-knowledge is the wisdom he was given; jahilin means acting ignorantly, not lacking information.

outline.heading: His Lord answered him: an uplifting verse
outline.gist: After unbroken hardship, a verse that lifts the spirit.

outline.heading: The answer was prison
outline.gist: Having seen the signs, they jailed him to bury the scandal, and that was Allah's answer to his dua.

outline.heading: Mercy that looks like punishment: Khidr's ship and the boy
outline.gist: People mistake great mercies for misfortune, like the poor boat owner and the grieving parents.

outline.heading: How the injustice must have looked to Yusuf
outline.gist: Slandered and jailed for years for refusing sin, when yielding would have brought comfort and freedom.

outline.heading: Ethics has no 'considerations' as fiqh does
outline.gist: Fiqh weighs madhhab views; zina and injustice are simply forbidden at any age or circumstance.

outline.heading: The surah's aim is moral steadfastness
outline.gist: Yusuf never answered wrong with wrong, even when betrayed by those entrusted with him.

outline.heading: Do not justify your sins
outline.gist: If you fall, admit it with no excuse; justification blocks real repentance and repeats the sin.

outline.heading: We fight over fiqh and neglect agreed morals
outline.gist: The imams never differed on honesty, trust or zina; we split over minor fiqh while ethics decay.

outline.heading: You do not know what is mercy for you
outline.gist: A hardship may be the answer to a dua; your Lord has not abandoned you.

outline.heading: A new phase: entering prison
outline.gist: Each new passage raises Yusuf's character further.

outline.heading: Reading Hafs via the Shatibiyyah: the madd rules
outline.gist: Why separated madd is four counts here but shortened in his prayer recitation via Tayyibat al-Nashr; learn the long madd first.

outline.heading: Two young men enter prison with him
outline.gist: Recitation, and the meaning of fata as a young man; the harshness of being imprisoned.

outline.heading: Prison in Islamic law
outline.gist: A discretionary ta'zir penalty below the hudud, accepted only when beneficial and not for life-ruining terms.

outline.heading: Modern prisons and a society that produces criminals
outline.gist: Many inmates grew up in broken homes; Yusuf's steadfastness came from a prophetic upbringing.

outline.heading: Prisons as places of guidance
outline.gist: With nothing left to distract them, many inmates embrace Islam.

outline.heading: A true dream must recur
outline.gist: A single dream is not a ru'ya; it must repeat in the same form.

outline.heading: Dreams of the past and of the future; the false Ibn Sirin book
outline.gist: Most dreams interpret the past and few the future; the dream book attributed to Ibn Sirin is not his.

outline.heading: 'We see you among the muhsinin'
outline.gist: Between people, ihsan means visible competence and education, unlike Allah's sense of ihsan.

outline.heading: Ta'wil as interpretation
outline.gist: Ta'wil is explaining an image or event; news channels live on it and are always right after the fact.

outline.heading: Reading: before your food arrives
outline.gist: Recitation of Yusuf's reply.

outline.heading: First view: give me until the next meal
outline.gist: He needs time and questions about each man before interpreting.

outline.heading: Second view: the skill of inference
outline.gist: He can read even the meals' timing; inference like the shirt torn from behind.

outline.heading: Courtesy in speech before calling to Allah
outline.gist: He reassures them an answer is coming and asks leave to speak first, unlike callers who ignore the listener's need.

outline.heading: His first act in prison is dawah, not complaint
outline.gist: Unlike the 'where is Allah' protests heard in recent years, he does not object to his Lord.

outline.heading: He did not know how his story would end
outline.gist: We relax knowing the ending; he knew nothing of release, family or justice.

outline.heading: He could have told his own story
outline.gist: Instead of trading grievances or brushing them off, he took the chance to bring them to Allah.

outline.heading: 'That is from what my Lord taught me'
outline.gist: He credits Allah, not his own intelligence, for his knowledge.

outline.heading: Leaving the religion of a people who deny Allah and the hereafter
outline.gist: Egypt's mix of polytheist Copts and Hyksos who denied resurrection; seeing the surah whole.

outline.heading: Following the creed of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub
outline.gist: Recitation and explanation: never associating partners with Allah is a favour most do not thank.

outline.heading: Morality needs a creedal foundation
outline.gist: Your ethics follow from how you understand existence; borrowed ethics without their creed eventually fail.

outline.heading: A split between belief and conduct
outline.gist: Professing faith while lying and envying, or claiming ethics while seeing life as meaningless, cannot hold.

outline.heading: Even atheist philosophers admit the problem
outline.gist: Secular societies run on inherited Judeo-Christian ethics without the belief beneath them.

outline.heading: Yusuf grounds ethics in belief
outline.gist: Reread 12:37-38: his morality rests on having seen the proof of his Lord.

outline.heading: Outro

BORPM3_odmc.title: Tafseer of Surat 'Abasa, Part 1 (80:1-16)
BORPM3_odmc.one_line: Surat 'Abasa as Islam's ethical code: a single unseen frown, for a noble reason, recorded forever to set the bar of Muslim conduct.
BORPM3_odmc.summary: He frames the opening surahs of Juz Amma as the foundations of a way of life: where existence comes from, how to live it through the self, and finally the moral code, which 'Abasa supplies. Every ideology carries a morality, he argues, and borrowing Islamic-looking ethics without their divine root makes them decay into self-interest and mere appearance. After explaining the unusual verb-name and placing the surah in the early Makkan period, he tells the story. The Prophet was in a rare productive conversation with Quraysh leaders, taking on the harder, nobler task of winning freedom for dawah, when the blind Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum called out to him. He frowned for a moment, then went to him. No one saw it, the man could not see it, and no harm was done, yet the verses came that night. He stresses that this is not chastisement of a man known for always smiling, but a statement of the standard: Muslim morality is not judged only by harm, no one is beyond critique, and the ethical code is never compromised, even when exposure comes at the worst time. The verses teach that you do not know who will be purified, that the one who seeks deserves priority, and that the message is a dignified reminder never to be cheapened or forced on the unwilling.

wNSwFExYGz8.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Nazi'at (Part 3): Verses 34-46
wNSwFExYGz8.one_line: Closing An-Nazi'at: the overwhelming Hour, people judged by what they strove for, and outcomes tied to the state of the nafs.
wNSwFExYGz8.summary: After explaining how the final juz is a connected whole and recapping the surah's earlier sections, Pharaoh's self-deception and the verses that humble man before the heavens while declaring everything was made for him, the sheikh completes An-Nazi'at. Al-Taammah al-Kubra is the overwhelming, inescapable event, whose very sound conveys its weight, and it wipes out every worldly basis of status. On that day man remembers what he strove for, which makes intention central to judgment, and he warns how easily we normalize poor motives. Hellfire is brought into full view. The two outcomes follow inner states: whoever transgressed in arrogance and preferred the lowly life goes to Hellfire, while whoever feared standing before his Lord and restrained the self from desire reaches Paradise. He stresses that the dunya itself is not cursed, only a life lived for low desires, illustrated by the hadith of the distributed sheep and the Prophet's refusal to take more than a traveller's provision. On the final verses he warns against obsessing over the timing of the Hour and end-times speculation, since the Prophet's role is to warn, and he dwells on people feeling they lived only an evening or a morning. Life is short, and both the problem and the solution lie within the self.

outline.heading: Fearing the standing of one's Lord
outline.gist: Maqam means the gap in status between creation and Creator, which makes defiance unthinkable.

outline.heading: Restraining the self from desire

im9C2qDYLJM.title: Moderation #11: The Easy, Upright Way (al-Hanifiyyah al-Samhah)
im9C2qDYLJM.one_line: The most beloved way of religion to Allah is al-hanifiyyah al-samhah: an easy, forgiving turning away from falsehood toward truth.
im9C2qDYLJM.summary: Continuing the moderation series with a narration from the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, he looks at the Prophet's answer when asked which way of practising the religion is most beloved to Allah: al-hanifiyyah al-samhah. Before reaching it he gives a brief view that combining Isha with Maghrib in the late summer months deserves scholarly discussion for people with early mornings, while warning that it makes no sense if people then stay up late anyway. He clarifies that the question was not which religion is beloved but which manner of practice. He then unpacks the two words. Hanif comes from a root meaning to bend or incline away, so the image is of someone on a course who gently steers off the path of falsehood toward the right one, not someone who breaks away violently or rigidly. Samhah carries openness of heart, forgiveness and ease: a person who is easy to talk to, negotiate with and disagree with. Together the phrase draws a picture of a non-threatening, non-intimidating movement toward truth. He presents this as a description of what the deen is and how Allah wants it carried: we were guided to righteousness by a path that is not harsh or unforgiving, and Allah loves to see people live it that way, as the Prophet did.

AlYUTIqs5wQ.title: Moderation #6: Allah Does Not Need You to Harm Yourself
AlYUTIqs5wQ.one_line: The old man who vowed to walk to Hajj: self-harm dressed up as worship breaks the balance and fabric of Islam.
AlYUTIqs5wQ.summary: Continuing the series on balance, the sheikh tells the hadith of the Prophet seeing an elderly man being carried along between his two sons. When told the man had vowed to walk as an act of devotion, the Prophet said Allah has no need for this man to torment himself, and ordered him to ride. The sheikh stresses that walking is not itself an act of worship, and that even the prayer may be offered seated by someone who is ill, so there is no basis for hurting oneself and burdening one's children in the name of piety. He argues that the moment the religion makes room for harmful acts presented as closeness to Allah, Islam loses its fabric and stops working, because harm to oneself, to others, or to one's ability to function and to fulfil real obligations is excluded by design. He gives the example of chronically ill people, such as diabetics with failing kidneys, who insist on fasting every Ramadan and get angry when told not to. They should pay the expiation if they can, and otherwise simply do the worship they are able to. He closes hoping that Islamic literacy in the community will rise so that such behaviour fades.

outline.gist: Each Ramadan ill people insist on fasting and resent being told not to; they should pay expiation if able and do the worship they can.

outline.heading: Raising Islamic literacy
outline.gist: Allowing religious people to hurt themselves and others costs Islam its balance; he hopes better literacy will reduce this.

vsIYCoLzM7U.title: From Populations to Communities: Political Centralization
vsIYCoLzM7U.one_line: Closing the series: Muslims cannot centralize politics here, but can unify advocacy, and serving the local community is the greatest service to the ummah.
vsIYCoLzM7U.summary: Wrapping up his series on turning a population into a community, he says religious political parties are neither legal nor desirable in Canada, but advocacy can be centralized. He recalls a few months when every masjid in the city followed the same advocacy groups and acted as one, the only time in his years here he felt that, and contrasts it with the lack of organized advocacy on domestic civil rights, which left Muslims exposed to harmful legislation and to curriculum and parental-rights issues. He then attacks moral grandstanding: talking big about the ummah and global causes while neglecting the needy right beside you is a way to look virtuous without tiring local work. The opposite extreme, not caring at all, is just as bad. The balance is to change the big picture by fixing what you can influence, as the Prophet did by building a functional society in Madinah that survived his death and spread worldwide. A strong local community is the greatest service to the ummah; young people should invest in their education and skills now. He admits wartime fundraisers largely eased our guilt, insists this country offers unmatched freedom to build, and says nothing but our own unwillingness, lack of grit and selflessness stands in the way.

c1TVNJxhYf4.title: Moderation #5: The Three Men and the Prophet's Sunnah
c1TVNJxhYf4.one_line: The three men who vowed endless worship show that bid'ah is an imbalance that destroys functionality, not merely something the Prophet did not do.
c1TVNJxhYf4.summary: The sheikh presents the hadith of the three men who asked the Prophet's wives about his worship, found it modest, and reasoned that he did not need more since his sins were forgiven. One vowed to fast every day, one to pray all night, one never to marry. He first argues that this hadith, usually cited on bid'ah, shows that bid'ah is best understood through the lens of balance: an innovation exaggerates one aspect of the religion at the expense of another so that the objectives are no longer achieved. Arguing only that the Prophet or companions did not do something is weak, since much that we do today was never done then, and it leaves people unable to pinpoint real errors or to be lenient where lenience is due. He laments that the community is stuck between rigid and hollow extremes. The three men were sincere and impressive by worldly standards, but their plans would destroy functionality: no sleep means no work, no marriage means no families, constant fasting means a weak body. The Prophet corrected their false premise, saying he is the most God-fearing and does exactly what is needed, and that whoever turns from his sunnah is not of him.

outline.heading: A hadith used for both bid'ah and balance
outline.gist: Scholars cite this famous hadith on bid'ah, but bid'ah and moderation are closely tied.

outline.heading: Bid'ah as imbalance that misses the objective
outline.gist: Innovation exaggerates one aspect of Islam over another so the religion's objectives are not achieved.

outline.heading: Why 'the Prophet didn't do it' is a weak argument
outline.gist: Many things we do were never done then; this argument hides real errors and blocks legitimate lenience.

outline.heading: Stuck between two extremes
outline.gist: The community is trapped between the rigid and the hollow, while Islam itself lies between them.

outline.heading: The three men and their flawed logic
outline.gist: They found the Prophet's worship modest, assumed he needed less, and vowed constant fasting, night prayer and celibacy.

outline.heading: Sincere but destructive of functionality
outline.gist: Their dedication is impressive, but no sleep, no marriage and no eating would weaken the person and the ummah.

outline.heading: The Prophet corrects their premise
outline.gist: He is the most God-fearing and does the optimal: he sleeps and prays, fasts and breaks fast, and marries.

outline.heading: Whoever turns from my sunnah is not of me
outline.gist: Making up a new way of living that removes Islam's balance is the real problem, and they returned to equilibrium.

outline.heading: Outro

qhuPs5n0L2Y.speaker: adnan
qhuPs5n0L2Y.speaker_note: refers to his 13 years in London, his Syrian village imam and the London Council of Imams
qhuPs5n0L2Y.title: From Populations to Communities: Religious Centralization
qhuPs5n0L2Y.one_line: The third pillar of community: centralized, respected religious leadership, with Jumuah as Allah's built-in system for uniting and mobilizing Muslims.
qhuPs5n0L2Y.summary: In this series on turning a population into a community, the sheikh names the third centralization: religious affairs. The only functional Muslim communities he has seen, his Syrian village under an imam who built its clinic, schools and river banks, and certain Damascus mosques, had trusted, unified religious leadership. Historically scholars checked political power, and the great imams Abu Hanifah, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad were jailed or lashed for refusing to serve rulers, yet their communities trusted them. He insists he is not asking for uniformity or for respect for himself, and notes he has never spoken ill of a scholar, since discrediting scholars weakens the religion itself, as seen in faiths whose followers ignore their intact scriptures. A community needs local religious references, not random online voices. Jumuah is a God-installed system that obliges everyone to gather weekly and hear direction, yet thousands of khutbahs in the city change little. In the second khutbah he notes that governments understood this power, jailing outspoken imams and, in Syria, attacking the Friday crowds. He cites the hadith that knowledge departs when scholars are taken, and urges respect for scholars, belonging to the ummah, and raising the next generation of them.

outline.heading: Opening
The third centralization: religious affairs
outline.gist: The functional communities he has known, small groups in Muslim-majority countries, were held together by centralized religious leadership alone.

outline.heading: The imam who built his village
outline.gist: His village imam of thirty years funded and led nearly every meaningful institution, from the clinic to the river banks.

outline.heading: Scholars as the check on rulers

outline.heading: The four imams who stood up to power
outline.gist: Abu Hanifah died in prison, Malik was lashed, al-Shafi'i was nearly condemned and Ahmad was jailed, yet they preserved the community's values.

outline.heading: Never speaking ill of scholars
outline.gist: He has never maligned a scholar, since weakening religious references weakens the deen and leaves everyone carrying it alone.

outline.heading: Religions that keep the book but not its teachings
outline.gist: Billions can keep a scripture yet follow none of it once its references are discredited.

outline.heading: Not uniformity but respect for references
outline.gist: Disagreement and questions are welcome; what is needed is respect for those who carry religious leadership.

outline.heading: Local references, not a voice on YouTube
outline.gist: Learning from scholars anywhere is fine, but a community needs its own religious centre.

outline.heading: Jumuah as a God-installed leadership system
outline.gist: Everyone must attend and listen weekly, and Muslims in a new city first look for a masjid and a Jumuah.

outline.heading: A billion listeners every week
outline.gist: The weekly gathering could channel the energy of a billion Muslims in one direction, yet it has been neutralized.

outline.heading: Respect is for the message, not the person
outline.gist: Respect shown to the minbar is respect for the Quran it carries; refusing any centralization only weakens oneself.

outline.heading: Why a city council of imams
outline.gist: The London Council of Imams exists to centralize religious affairs and protect the community from extreme narratives in any direction.

outline.heading: Thousands of khutbahs, the same complaints
outline.gist: Standing on the minbar is a grave responsibility, yet thousands hear khutbahs weekly and the same complaints persist for decades.

outline.heading: Built-in mobilization and senior local scholars
outline.gist: Jumuah already gives the reach no marketing could buy, and the city has scholars with decades of teaching; this piece should be achievable.

outline.heading: Interlude
What the word imam means
outline.gist: Imam means leader and has no other meaning.

outline.heading: Governments neutralized the imams
outline.gist: Regimes jailed imams with opinions because they understood the power of centralized religious leadership.

outline.heading: Syria: the Friday crowds
outline.gist: The uprising went out from the mosques after Jumuah, which is why the regime shut the country on Fridays and targeted mosques.

outline.heading: Coordination and respect for the minbar
outline.gist: A little collaboration and getting over our egos under the care of the masjid could change a community.

outline.heading: Knowledge departs when scholars are taken
outline.gist: Allah removes knowledge by taking the scholars until people follow the ignorant and go astray.

outline.heading: No papacy, but you belong to an ummah
outline.gist: You need not accept everything scholars say, but you cannot go rogue; cherish them and build the next generation.

outline.heading: Scholars are the heirs of the prophets
outline.gist: The prophets left knowledge, not wealth, as their inheritance.

outline.heading: Outro
